entry.title: Spotify Rolls Out AI Persona Badges, Removes 75 Million “Spammy Tracks”
entry.summary: Over the summer, Spotify finally announced a plan to deal with the onslaught of AI slop, which involved “AI Persona” badges for AI-generated artists and keeping their music out of recommended playlists. In a new statement, the streaming service says they’ve removed over 75 million “spammy tracks” from the platform. The statement also says they’ve…
entry.content:
Over the summer, Spotify finally announced a plan to deal with the onslaught of AI slop, which involved "AI Persona" badges for AI-generated artists and keeping their music out of recommended playlists. In a new statement, the streaming service says they've removed over 75 million "spammy tracks" from the platform.

The statement also says they've pulled more than 50 million slop and spam tracks out of recommendations and labeled thousands of artist profiles with AI Persona badges. In addition, artists who release AI-assisted songs have the option to identify AI in the song credits.

"No single signal catches slop or spam on its own, so we combine many: listener engagement and feedback, upload patterns, metadata, and information from multiple third-party AI detection tools," the statement reads. "AI detection technology in particular has limitations, and it will only get harder as generative AI evolves. Using these signals together, we can identify likely slop or spam with more confidence. We also hunt for new tactics, including mass uploads, duplicates, SEO manipulation, spammy playlist networks, and artificially short tracks. As spammers change tactics, we'll keep updating our systems."

Read the full statement here.

entry.title: Romain Gavras Addresses Slop Copies Of GENER8ION & Yung Lean “Storm” Video
entry.summary: Last month, Yung Lean made his US television debut with a recreation of his and GENER8ION’s viral “Storm” music video at the VMAs. The hypnotic choreography captures the Swedish rapper/singer standing and smoking a cigarette in the middle of 66 dancing boys, and the live performance was even more mesmerizing. The video was shot by…
entry.content:
Last month, Yung Lean made his US television debut with a recreation of his and GENER8ION's viral "Storm" music video at the VMAs. The hypnotic choreography captures the Swedish rapper/singer standing and smoking a cigarette in the middle of 66 dancing boys, and the live performance was even more mesmerizing. The video was shot by legendary French film director Romain Gavras, who expressed his disappointment in AI-generated slop imitations of the video that have ensued.

In a conversation with Vulture, Gavras says his daughter was the first to show him an imitation, which featured dogs. At first he thought it was cute, until the trend took an edgy turn, incorporating Elon Musk, Kim Jong-un, Hitler, Jeffrey Epstein, and the like. "It made me sad for all the people who put in so much work on our video," Gavras told Vulture. "A trend like this can make even good work look lame. Part of me wanted to quit filmmaking, move back to Greece, and become an olive farmer."

Vulture points out that many of the imitations were made using a tool called Genjutsu, which was released in late August by the AI video company Higgsfield. A few AI companies have even approached Gavras about licensing "Storm," but he declined. There's little possibility for him to take legal action against the imitations, as that would mean suing each user partaking in the trend. Besides, he maintains that none of them are close to the original anyway: "They're missing the swagger of Yung Lean," he says. "He looks like a dangerous baby. There's something in the imperfection of humanity, and the interior life of someone who dances or even someone who just smokes a cigarette, that's not quite there yet. But who the fuck knows what will happen in a year."

Read the full interview here.

entry.content:
Last month, Bicep returned with three tracks: "Air," "Lemonder," and "Viper." Today, the UK-based electronic duo is announcing their new album SLUG, which follows their CHROMA series. Now, they're releasing three more songs: "Gas," "Ultra," and "Equarium."

The title SLUG was inspired by the contrast between land and sea slugs. "It felt like an amazing metaphor: you think one thing, but actually there's a whole world beyond what you initially perceive," the group says. The album is full of guests, as are today's singles. "Gas" features Lauren Duffus and SOARR; "Ultra" features Eartheater and Saskia; and "Equarium" features Kehina.

The new tracks also come with a three-part short film developed by director Alex Takács. About it, Takács says:

A while back, I read this article about a very expensive racing pigeon that was stolen in Brussels. It led me into this obsessive world of pigeon breeding, where it's all about bloodlines. The technology to control pigeons in flight is also real. There's a duality and terrible beauty in all that, and it just felt right for these singles.

Bicep add:

When it came to the music videos, we wanted to broaden the themes we were working on in the studio into other media. The films let us take that outside the music itself. Free parties, pigeon fanciers, demolition derbies — they're very different worlds, but they're all niche interests existing outside the mainstream, with their own combinations of beauty, darkness and chaos. There's something about shining a light on those worlds that feels very connected to SLUG.

Watch the three-part short film below.

entry.content:
Last year, Doves shared their sixth studio album Constellations For The Lonely. Today, Jez Williams is announcing his debut solo LP, Life Of Me And You. The guitarist of the post-Britpop band is sharing the lead single "Hollow Man" today.

"Without resorting to clichés, 'Hollow Man' is about our modern life," he explains. "It can just so easily take the soul out of you. Too much information, too many opinions, too much change coming from all angles. Tsunamis of information coming at you. It can be overwhelming. It makes you less present and makes you more in your head. I thought to put all of that to a sort of AC/DC-style riff, breaking out into a wider chorus. It all just came out in one go."

Life Of Me And You was written, recorded, and produced by Williams in various studios. Check out "Hollow Man" below.

entry.title: Wendy Eisenberg & more eaze Announce Debut Whait Album sympathy at home: Hear “Falling Down”
entry.summary: Wendy Eisenberg and more ease are both prolific collaborators who do a lot of work in New York’s experimental circles, and they’ve crossed paths plenty of times over the years. Back in 2024, Eisenberg and more eaze formed a duo called Whait, and they released their debut song “calm down” on Just Cause Vol. 1,…
entry.content:
Wendy Eisenberg and more ease are both prolific collaborators who do a lot of work in New York's experimental circles, and they've crossed paths plenty of times over the years. Back in 2024, Eisenberg and more eaze formed a duo called Whait, and they released their debut song "calm down" on Just Cause Vol. 1, a benefit compilation that raised money for the Palestine Children's Relief Fund. Today, they announce plans for Whait's full-length debut, which is called sympathy at home and which comes out next year.

Right now, both Wendy Eisenberg are plenty busy. Eisenberg, a member of groups like Editrix and the Bill Orcutt Guitar Quartet, went in more of a bucolic but playful singer-songwriter direction on the great self-titled album that they released earlier this year. Mari Rubio, the musician who records as more eaze, contributed to that record, and Eisenberg played on sentence structure in the country, one of two new albums that more eaze released this year.

Eisenberg and more eaze recorded most of sympathy at home at their New York studios when they were in between tours, and lead single "Falling Down" has some of the same playful, off-kilter folk sensibility as Eisenberg's self-titled album. It's a florid, conversational acoustic number with overlapping harmonies and just a bit of glitch in its DNA. Check it out below.

entry.title: Ellie Goulding Apologizes For Promoting Diamonds From Mine On Indigenous Land
entry.summary: Earlier this month, the UK pop star Ellie Goulding appeared at a London store opening from the jewelry band Boodles and modeled some of their pink diamonds. Upon learning that those diamonds came from the Argyle diamond mine, located on Indigenous land in Western Australia, Goulding, a noted environmental advocate, has apologized for failing to…
entry.content:
Earlier this month, the UK pop star Ellie Goulding appeared at a London store opening from the jewelry band Boodles and modeled some of their pink diamonds. Upon learning that those diamonds came from the Argyle diamond mine, located on Indigenous land in Western Australia, Goulding, a noted environmental advocate, has apologized for failing to uphold her own values.

Goulding shared an apologetic statement with the Mirror, saying:

Protecting the environment is a cause close to my heart. I always strive to uphold those values. Regretfully, in this instance, I fell short. I was not aware of the concerns surrounding the Argyle mine, and I am grateful that it has been brought to my attention.

You will certainly not see me wearing diamonds originating from the Argyle mine again. The Indigenous and local communities affected deserve better. While I am mortified to have made this error in judgement, I am letting this moment serve as a reminder and an opportunity to continue to question the status quo, to learn and do better.

As the Mirror reports, a week before the Boodles store opening that Goulding attended, the company bought the Argyle pink diamonds from the mining company Rio Tanto, which maintained the Argyle mine, earlier this month. The company shut down the mine itself in 2020, after 37 years of production. Indigenous activists in the area have long warned of the devastating environmental effects of the Argyle mine, and Goulding herself has accused mining companies of "destroying" ancestral lands.

At the Boodles store opening, Goulding served as guest of honor and said that the pink diamonds were "so elegant and iconic." There's certainly some dissonance between that and her various roles as an environmental advocate, for which she was made an MBE earlier this year. She also serves as an ambassador for the WWF, the environmental organization that has cautioned celebrities against endorsing luxury good without researching the impacts that they make. In a statement, the WWF says, "Ellie is a passionate advocate for nature and human rights and has championed the rights of Indigenous peoples as a WWF ambassador. We have discussed this issue with Ellie and continue to value her support."

In a statement to The Guardian, the Gelganyem Group, which represents the Indigenous people who serve as the land's traditional owners, says, "Gelganyem chair Kia Dowell, a Gija woman, acknowledges Ellie Goulding’s apology and welcomes her recognition that Indigenous and local communities deserve better. She hopes it helps the public and Rio Tinto shareholders understand what is at stake at Argyle and the standard Rio Tinto’s mine closure must meet."

entry.title: They Are Gutting A Body Of Water’s Doug Dulgarian Reveals Cancer Diagnosis, Cancels Tour
entry.summary: Some really scary and awful news: Doug Dulgarian, frontman of the hugely important Philadelphia band They Are Gutting A Body Of Water and founder of the equally important indie label Julia’s War, has been diagnosed with cancer. Dulgarian, the guy wearing a striped shirt in the above photo, made the announcement in a heartfelt Instagram…
entry.content:
Some really scary and awful news: Doug Dulgarian, frontman of the hugely important Philadelphia band They Are Gutting A Body Of Water and founder of the equally important indie label Julia's War, has been diagnosed with cancer. Dulgarian, the guy wearing a striped shirt in the above photo, made the announcement in a heartfelt Instagram post this morning, writing that he got his diagnosis on Friday, the same day that TAGABOW released the massive new mixtape KOOL FAITH / LOOSIES II. TAGABOW were scheduled to launch a North American tour on Thursday night in Baltimore, but that won't happen now. In his very candid post, though, Dulgarian says that "the prognosis seems to be pretty good."

In light of the tour cancellation, Dulgarian's friends have launched a GoFundMe campaign to help out with medical expenses, as well as the lost income from the tour. Dulgarian does not say what kind of cancer he's battling — merely that he will start treatment "in a couple weeks." He also says that the band will "keep the Philly & nyc dates on the schedule" — that's Dec. 10 at Warsaw and Dec. 18 at Union Transfer — "in hopes I’ll be able to do it." In his post, Dulgarian repeatedly emphasizes that he think he'll be fine, that his diagnosis "ain’t the end of the world." It's worth your time to read what he has written:

damn. super bummed to have to talk about this. and super bummed to do this

I was diagnosed with cancer last Friday, same day we put out Kool Faith. crazy day, every possible emotion lmao

we obviously can’t do the tour, as I need to get this figured out. i have treatment in a couple weeks

I have a feeling it will all work out. been thru a lot of things in my crazy and (atp) relatively long existence and im no stranger to putting my best foot forward and facing some difficult shit

I wanna make this clear. im not seeking pity. i do not want to sway your emotions to feel bad for me. I just want to inform you. I genuinely believe this will work out just fine. there are many people with much worse problems and my life has been so infinitely blessed and privileged & I never lose sight of that

also I don’t think that kind of mindset is beneficial. if I start to believe that i deserve pity from others, I would feel bad for myself, & that’s the beginning of giving up

this ain’t the end of the world

we’re gonna keep the Philly & nyc dates on the schedule in hopes I’ll be able to do it

lifes so weird man. im a firm believer that everything happens for a reason. most of the time i don’t understand why at the time, but it always makes sense in the end. im sure this situation is no different

the fact that i got the diagnosis the same day we put out a massive compilation featuring as many friends as i could muster, well that symbolism that is not lost on me

I know I can be real corny sometimes but music and community has given me a purpose in my life that I didn’t have before I found it. you live one time and I haven’t got time to not mean everything I say, or to leave things unsaid

i love nothing more than making music and seeing my friends & it breaks my heart to cancel a tour

I hope what I can walk away with from this situation is gratitude for another experience. ive been blessed to experience a full spectrum of emotion in my life. very good, very bad, a whole lot in between

im scared and unsure of how this will all go. the prognosis seems to be pretty good. thats cool

love yall

I’ll keep ya posted

-doug

Doug Dulgarian has already been through a lot of trials in his life, and he talked about it in a Stereogum feature last year. He's a real one and an important figure, and we wish him a speedy and comfortable recovery.

entry.title: Public Acid Release Deranged New EP Pay No More
entry.summary: When shows started happening again in summer 2021, my first one back was a guerrilla hardcore punk gig in Richmond, held in an outdoor location remote enough that people were lighting off fireworks in the pit without worrying that they were going to get it all shut down. The Richmond-via-Raleigh band Public Acid headlined that…
entry.content:
When shows started happening again in summer 2021, my first one back was a guerrilla hardcore punk gig in Richmond, held in an outdoor location remote enough that people were lighting off fireworks in the pit without worrying that they were going to get it all shut down. The Richmond-via-Raleigh band Public Acid headlined that show and played an absolutely insane set, and I owe them my allegiance forever. I'm delighted to report that their new record captures some of that intensity.

This is nothing new for Public Acid, whose 2024 LP Deadly Struggle was one of my favorite hardcore albums of the year. Their new record Pay No More is a sloppy, chaotic basement-punk attack. There's nothing routine about it. I guess you could analyze it, looking for influences from Japanese or Scandinavian hardcore or whatever. But I'd recommend experiencing it as a raw, primal blurt. You can do that below.

There's another new release today that should scratch a similar itch, too. Invertebrates are a Richmond hardcore punk band who share a few members with Public Acid and who put out records on the same label, Beach Impediment. They play a lot of shows together, too. Invertebrates' style is a little more direct and straightforward, and I might actually like them just a tiny bit more, but the two bands obviously complement the hell out of each other. Today, Invertebrates follow their 2024 LP Sick To Survive with a new EP of their own, an urgent but seriously fun seven-song blast called Accosted. Check it out below.

Pay No More and Accosted are both out now on Beach Impediment.

entry.content:
I truly cannot believe we're about to get a new Disfear record. In the past two years, two members of the legendary Swedish D-beat band, vocalist Tomas Lindberg and drummer Marcus Andersson, passed away from cancer. (Another member, bassist Henke Frykman, also died of cancer in 2011.) The band's last album was 2008's Live The Storm, an absolute classic, and that would've made a powerful farewell. But before Lindberg and Andersson died, Disfear recorded one more album, and it's coming out next month.

Disfear recorded The Last Nail, their final album, with Converge's Kurt Ballou, and we've already posted "Early Graves," a lead single with an extremely on-the-nose title. Today, Disfear share the anthemic new track "Shackled To Our Vice." The magic of this band is that a song like this can sound fun and triumphant, even amid the tragic context of its release. Listen below.

The Last Nail is out 11/20 on Relapse.

entry.summary: The young London band Alphabet have a sleek but atmospheric post-punk sound that really recalls some of the critical favorites of the ’00s. They first landed on our radar with their single “Sense” earlier this year, and now they’ve followed it with “Into The Blur,” a broody and itchy new track that somehow reminds me…
entry.content:
The young London band Alphabet have a sleek but atmospheric post-punk sound that really recalls some of the critical favorites of the '00s. They first landed on our radar with their single "Sense" earlier this year, and now they've followed it with "Into The Blur," a broody and itchy new track that somehow reminds me of both Interpol and Love Is All, two bands who don't really share anything in common other than the fact that they existed at the same time.

Guitarist Tom Sullivan produced and mixed "Into The Blur," and singer/bassist Lena Pishofer did the artwork. In a press release, Pishofer says, "'Into The Blur' is a memory of a period in my early 20s — a time when I was pretty unhappy but also felt very creatively alive. It’s about getting older and realizing you’ll never feel quite the same way again. I don’t necessarily want to go back to how it was, but I miss the freedom and not really knowing where life was going. It’s about wanting to be there just once more." Check it out below.

entry.title: Soul Glo – “Ppl Worried” (Feat. Tunde Adebimpe)
entry.summary: Early next year, the bugged-out Philadelphia punk band Soul Glo will finally return with NA I’M GON GRAB ALLAT, the long-awaited follow-up to their 2002 instant classic Diaspora Problems. The new record is really shaping up to be something, too. We’ve already posted lead single “February Theory,” an unhinged freakout with trace elements of club…
entry.content:
Early next year, the bugged-out Philadelphia punk band Soul Glo will finally return with NA I’M GON GRAB ALLAT, the long-awaited follow-up to their 2002 instant classic Diaspora Problems. The new record is really shaping up to be something, too. We've already posted lead single "February Theory," an unhinged freakout with trace elements of club music threaded throughout. Today, Soul Glo have another new song, and it's a collaboration with TV On The Radio's Tunde Adebimpe.

The mere fact of Tunde Adebimpe singing on a Soul Glo song is fucking awesome. It's like a much smaller-scale version of whatn TV On The Radio had David Bowie on "Province" 20 years ago. Much like TVOTR, Soul Glo don't stop sounding like themselves just because they're working with a legend. Their new song, "Ppl Worried," is a thundering, erratic lurch about snorting coke and scaring the people around you: "Love enters through the nose! The nostril's my favorite hole! I can't fucking quit it, bro!" The song sounds coked-out, too. The thundering drums and "fuck it" chants really hit, and I love how Pierce Jordan slides into his feral rap delivery.

Pierce Jordan's not the only guest on NA I’M GON GRAB ALLAT, either. It's also got contributions from Oxbow's Eugene Robinson, Commitment’s Tati Salazar, Mannequin Pussy's Colins "Bear" Regisford, and rappers MIKE and Bbymutha. Also, Soul Glo are currently on tour with Chat Pile and Shallowater, so you should go see them if you can. Check out "Ppl Worried" below.

NA I’M GON GRAB ALLAT is out 1/15 on Epitaph.

entry.title: One Step Closer Announce New Album Zero: Hear Two Tracks
entry.summary: A few years ago, the young Wilkes-Barre band One Step Closer came out sprinting with a fiery, sincere form of melodic hardcore that recalled past eras without ever putting quotation marks around what they were doing. entry.content:
A few years ago, the young Wilkes-Barre band One Step Closer came out sprinting with a fiery, sincere form of melodic hardcore that recalled past eras without ever putting quotation marks around what they were doing. They were a Stereogum Band To Watch back in 2021, and then they moved in a more expansive direction on their 2024 sophomore album All You Embrace. After dropping the one-off single "Jinx" last year, One Step Closer are ready to announce a whole new album called Zero.

One Step Closer recorded Zero with Drug Chuch/Drain collaborator Jon Markson, a producer who knows how to combine hardcore crunch with big, searing hooks. The band says that they found the record's sound by digging into what they call "older brother muisc," and a press release lists off a fun set of inspirations: "printing Mapquest directions to a VFW show, music video blocks on Steven’s Untitled Rock Show, burned CDs with songs ripped from MySpace, and jumping a fence to sneak into Warped Tour in 2005."

With the album announcement, One Step Closer have shared two new songs, doing a double video for both of them. "Blue Hour" starts out slow and meditative and builds to en extremely satisfying fiery conclusion. "Was It Ever Enough?" goes more in the direction of the kind of fired-up, stagedive-happy emo that I associate with past One Step Closer tourmates Koyo and Anxious. Both songs are good! And I really like the video, which the band co-directed with Derek Rathbun. It follows a group of skater kids hanging out aimlessly, tagging the band's stencil logo on any available surface, and gathering at an outdoor live show where they all shoot off fireworks during the climactic moments of "Blue Hour."

Below, check out that video, as well as the two individual songs, the Zero tracklist, and One Step Closer's upcoming tour dates.

entry.title: Hannah Frances – “Circadian Heart”
entry.summary: “Circadian Heart,” the Vermont-based singer-songwriter Hannah Frances’ new single, pulls off a neat trick. It starts off as a playfully oblique folk song with supremely relaxed and assured vocal. As the song builds, more elements come in — impressionistic strings, jazz-influenced horns — and the song seems like it’s ready to whirl off into the…
entry.content:
"Circadian Heart," the Vermont-based singer-songwriter Hannah Frances' new single, pulls off a neat trick. It starts off as a playfully oblique folk song with supremely relaxed and assured vocal. As the song builds, more elements come in — impressionistic strings, jazz-influenced horns — and the song seems like it's ready to whirl off into the unknown. Instead, it keeps drawing itself back in, then expanding outward again. The song's structure is built on its own rhythm.

Last year, Hannah Frances released her album Nested In Tangles, and we were into it. Earlier this year, she collaborated with Mary Lattimore on "Beholden To The Birds Murmuring Above." At least for now, "Circadian Heart" is its own standalone single. In a press release, Frances says, "'Circadian Heart' is a look into the relational pattern of choosing unavailable people and trying to get them to choose me back, only to find that I have to stop chasing and learn to choose me in the end. How we’ll break our own hearts to feel familiar pain, until we choose a new way that is softer and more reciprocal."

Frances and director Derrick Alexander shot the "Circadian Heart" video in Illinois' Waterfall Glen State Park, and it's got a lot of lovely shots of Frances by a forest stream. Frances edited it herself. Check it out below, along with Frances' tour dates.

entry.content:
In May, sadie released her enticing debut album Better Angels, which earned her our Artist To Watch honor. The Brooklyn singer-songwriter and producer is back today with a shimmering new earworm called "Little Things."

"This is a song about living in the moment and not getting too existential about things," the artist explains. "It's about not worrying what’s going to happen next. I was feeling sexy and flirty when I wrote it and it's probably the only purely feel-good song I’ve ever written and may ever write…"

"Little Things" is another gem that weaves together guitars, synths, and strings into a hypnotic, groovy wave of sound. Listen below.

entry.title: claire rousay & zander raymond Announce New Album something good: Hear “can’t we have both”
entry.summary: Fun fact: If you subscribe to Thrill Jockey’s Substack, you sometimes get to hear new music before anyone else. Last week the label quietly announced something good, a new album-length collaboration from LA “emo ambient” hero claire rousay and multi-disciplinary artist zander raymond, whose music shares rousay’s interest in found sound and painfully gorgeous drone.…
entry.content:
Fun fact: If you subscribe to Thrill Jockey's Substack, you sometimes get to hear new music before anyone else. Last week the label quietly announced something good, a new album-length collaboration from LA "emo ambient" hero claire rousay and multi-disciplinary artist zander raymond, whose music shares rousay's interest in found sound and painfully gorgeous drone. (Check out last year's no one notices the fly.) They even provided an advance stream of lead single "can't we have both." This email arrived at a time when I was scrambling to finish some other work, and then it passed me by. So I'm happy that today the official album announcement has arrived.

Thrill Jockey will release something good in January. The album blurs the edges between abstract sound explorations and pop structure, a mixture demonstrated on "can't we have both." The track is shimmering and shapeless, yet rousay gives it form with her return to lead vocals, providing lyrics that lend further emotional weight to an achingly beautiful piece of music. "Feeling washed up in the used CD store," she begins. "It’s a burden, it’s a triumph/ My industry evaporates and it doesn’t need me anymore." Against a gradually intensifying backdrop, she builds to a tough conclusion: "I don't know if I belong here anymore."

It's a prolific time for rousay, who just released her on holding EP last week and dropped an album with Martyna Basta shortly before that. But when is it not a prolific time for rousay? Hear "can't we have both" below.

something good is out 1/29 on Thrill Jockey. Pre-order it here.

entry.title: Jay-Z Reportedly Picks Himself For Super Bowl Halftime Show, U2 To Play Thanksgiving Eve Game
entry.summary: We can’t exactly act like this was a surprise, can we? Jay-Z’s company Roc Nation has produced every Super Bowl Halftime Show since 2020. The NFL brought Jay in as a transparent attempt to get past the moment where players like Colin Kaepernick were protesting against police violence, and the partnership has been awfully successful…
entry.content:
We can't exactly act like this was a surprise, can we? Jay-Z's company Roc Nation has produced every Super Bowl Halftime Show since 2020. The NFL brought Jay in as a transparent attempt to get past the moment where players like Colin Kaepernick were protesting against police violence, and the partnership has been awfully successful for everyone involved. The last two Super Bowls, in particular, have had Kendrick Lamar and Bad Bunny at the moments when those two artists were fully in control of the zeitgeist. Now, we have reached the inevitable moment where Jay, at least according to reports, has chosen himself as the Halftime Show headliner.

In recent months, there have been rumors about other possible Super Bowl artists like Miley Cyrus and Justin Bieber, but Jay-Z always loomed in the background of those stories. Now, multiple sources have reportedly told Puck News that Jay has selected himself for the 2027 Super Bowl. Jay recently returned to the stage for the first time in years, playing a series of stadium shows around the world, including a trio of high-profile hometown gigs at Yankee Stadium, and he rapped on a remix of his wife Beyoncé's single "Morning Dew (Donk)" — his first new on-record verse in two years. Also, the woman who sued him for sexual assault recently recanted her allegations. The 56-year-old Jay certainly doesn't need to make a comeback, but if he feels like make some more music, he has certainly created the conditions where it could resonate.

In other halftime show news, the NFL continues to explore ways to use big-deal musicians to draw attention to their non-Super Bowl games. The biggest of those was Christmas 2024, when Beyoncé staged a big Cowboy Carter performance at a Netflix-televised game. Today, Netflix announced that U2, currently gearing up for a new album and tour, will play the halftime show "the NFL's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game." The LA Rams will host the Green Bay Packers 11/25 at SoFi Stadium, with the game starting at 8 p.m. U2 famously played the first post-9/11 Super Bowl in 2002, so they're old hands at this.

entry.title: An iPhone Is Their Acoustic Guitar
entry.summary: It started with the rise of the elusive duo ear. On their recent album Rumspringa, Jonah Paz and Yaelle Avtan’s iPhone recordings feel simultaneously like a ripped page out of a scribbled diary and a dilapidated house party anthem, as if the album is safeguarding secrets but is also fickle in how it carries them.…
entry.content:
It started with the rise of the elusive duo ear. On their recent album Rumspringa, Jonah Paz and Yaelle Avtan’s iPhone recordings feel simultaneously like a ripped page out of a scribbled diary and a dilapidated house party anthem, as if the album is safeguarding secrets but is also fickle in how it carries them. Their music oscillates between bewitching stillness and hypnotic electronic scraps. 

Then came New York's Nicholas Gay and his Lockimara album Only Sun, Only Moon; and Nashville’s prolific Logan Hornyak, aka Melaina Kol, with his album Okay that’s a great idea if I do that then; and Eau Claire five-piece gash on their full-length at least you know what you’re laughing at; and the duo of Mikaela Oppenheimer and Hayden McGarvey, who just dropped their new EP The Point’s A Truss, My Trusselina under the moniker Trusselina. These artists all conjured some kind of digital rucksack sound, something that feels both introverted and extroverted. 

Moments across these releases range from electrifying to startlingly naked. Most songs occupy both poles. Melaina Kol’s “Bleater” transforms chopped vocals from Lowertown’s Olivia O. into something shamanic while string pricks are balanced by arco pulls of sustained notes. The effect is hushed and tactile, like hairs standing up on the back of my neck. gash’s “Data Master” operates on noodling guitars, gear-shifting clangs, snagged vocal clips, and possessed whooshes before the track completely undresses with a standard drum kit and moody guitar strums. And, of course, there's Lockimara's "Lose Her," where Carolina Smith recites hopeless romantic lyrics: "Loser/ Always you'll lose your heart/ Stuck in your head phones/ Tapping the same beat/ Talk to me." The haptic assistance of piano and acoustic strums during the verses fall away for the euphoric non-chorus — a rhythmic explosion of metallic clanks with her voice spliced in the background. Whatever she divulges amidst an explosive drumbeat and billowing synths evaporates.

I’ve become increasingly fixated on this sound where the tendrils of folk and the wires of electronic glitch music get tangled. For months I’ve been twirling the words "glitch folk" around my head. There was even a blog post where I gave the term "intimatelectro" a test run. This series of albums has felt simultaneously nostalgic and innovative, with the signatures of fragile voices, testy electronics, warm acoustic instruments, or transfixing melodies.

The nostalgic essence stems from resemblances to 2000s acts like the Postal Service, Frou Frou, múm, Architecture in Helsinki, Atlas Sound, maybe even Ariel Pink. The term "laptop twee" has been thrown around to a nauseating degree lately, with ear often in the conversation. This essay is not about that, but it maybe nestles up to similar concepts. "Twee" almost seems oxymoronic when describing these albums, especially compared to the sounds of Ben Lee or Boy Least Likely To. Whereas there are echoes of the quaint aesthetic movement in certain melodies and textures, these albums are much more gnarled and violent in how they carry their coziness.

The sense of intimacy within these tracks doesn’t get canceled out by the bleeps and bloops. In fact, the internet melodies and iPhone-scrappage sampling makes the music feel all the more human because of their imperfections and raggedness. The sound of a machine breaking down, searching for clarity feels like something alive — something closer to being inside a human brain in 2026. Everything feels chaotic, yet whole. Our world has expanded in lengths we can’t keep up with, were never meant to. Everything feels tangential and also cyclic. It’s a Rube Goldberg Machine sound. 

With their blurry, subversive approach to sampling, these bands have further confused what intimacy sounds like. Whereas some acts like gash use a mix of personal recordings, ear are cagier about their choices; the two members don't even reveal the sources of their samples to each other. By imprinting their tracks with mysterious, lo-fi bursts of reality, they make the digital elements feel human and flawed.

ear’s “Water And Power” opens with echoey beats and tinkering percussion, followed by an obscure vocal sample and the softness of Paz and Avtan’s own vocals. This all happens within 10 seconds of the song’s opening. It’s so quick, but each element locks into place, moving on to the next captivating sound before we have a moment to process it. Neurons firing without our immediate awareness. It all leads to the sample of a woman harassing a man at a store checkout line. In the original clip, she demands he repent and talks about “fire and brimstone.” ear only use a small portion of it, snapping back into their airy vocals with the line “Somehow time is frozen/ And open and ali—." The vocals cut out like a call dropping service, and it’s unclear if they were going to say “alive” or “aligned.” The ambiguity is all the more powerful; in this world, most of the time it’s hard to have a complete thought. 

A cornerstone of this burgeoning sound is bedded in moments of quiet that burst into cacophonous swells, agonizing screams, or euphoric chorus builds. Sometimes the music feels dark and spiderwebby and reminiscent of the 2000s (the end of “Idola”). Maybe there's acoustic guitar, but that's not really what makes it folk. Instead, that essence arises from a DIY, stripped-down approach. An iPhone is their acoustic guitar — the ubiquitous instrument of confession. This music feels revealing, but you can't tell exactly what you're hearing. Even the most inscrutable gestures scan as intimate disclosures, especially as each person's identity becomes a cybernetic collage.

Then there’s the midwestern emo of it all — the long, strange titles and spontaneous combustion of screams, the oscillation between tender and volatile. It’s a constant pulse that feels eerily reminiscent of the optimization-obsessed times, constant motion that leaves us unable to process the noise. This music captures the feeling of the modern world moving too fast to understand life, to sink into the moment. By the end, with our bodies sore and our brains foggy, all we can do is scream.

But the more I’ve sat with this idea, I don’t believe this is a new genre emerging. Maybe it's a trend that's magnifying a resounding sentiment of the 2020s. These artists aren’t a part of the same scene, and most of the time their music doesn’t sound the same, but it does have a distinctive essence. I’ve also found it in the high-production polish of Phoebe Bridgers’ Lost Weekend and Chanel Beads’ latest Your Day Will Come, not to be confused with their 2024 album of the same name. Lost Weekend is an album about grief, dead futures, and haunted presents. I keep thinking of the use of voicemail from Bridgers' late father on "Never Going Back!" Gummy banjo strums rust alongside the brittle recording.

Either way, I’ve been trying to understand this feeling: when music seems intensely private but is hot-glued together from digital debris, unclear whether it's severed from public domain or unpocketed from personal databases. The contradiction of indie rock and IDM sounds battling each other within these songs captures what it’s like to post on Instagram, or any social media, today. You might be divulging something intimate or sentimental, but it’s at odds with the public performance of it all. It doesn’t make the sharing less true, but it does complicate the thinking that even a universal truth exists depending on the performance. 

Digging deeper into these artists' processes, it's clear that their priority is to animate the mistakes that are integral to their music's creation. Trusselina's Hayden McGarvey found a new direction after accidentally playing a recording backwards; gash's Logan Nyberg describes years of demos that were never necessarily intended to become a band. In both cases, the work arrives through the willingness to follow an idea before knowing what it might become. The mistake isn't just something left in the recording to make it feel human, but is part of the composition itself.

The more I try to draw connections between these artists, the more complicated writing about them becomes. ear, in particular, would probably hate this essay. They’ve discussed being wary of the identities that have accumulated around their music online, and of the ways an aesthetic can become associated with a particular scene or social world. That discomfort is totally valid. Perhaps the intimacy I hear across these records doesn't amount to a shared artistic philosophy at all. Perhaps it's a relationship being constructed by the listener, from fragments that were never intended to fit together, the same way these artists assemble their songs.

“A lot of IDM stuff is about speculation,” Avtan brought up in an interview from earlier this year. “It’s like, What is this random compilation with a random artist with a pseudonym? Those can be the most personal songs, because you can add so much meaning on top.” Mistakes and lack of context have been comforting lately. Maybe it's not only the sound of mistake, but stakes too. We're getting access to intimate sound and its risks of obfuscation. Our current world is fixated on easy access — a simple, untrustworthy AI-generated summary at every click. I've been thinking a lot about how we're at risk of taking clarity and easy answers for granted. Maybe this music is reaffirming because it's so intimately fragile and unknowing, which suggests humanity. Even with the electronic elements, it feels like an antidote for AI replication.

I know I am hearing this music differently in 2026 than I would have in 2006 or 2016. It might feel intoxicating because it’s a contradiction, electronic freak folk in the age of AI and commodified earnestness. Both ear and gash are adamant about maintaining the integrity of the process versus the perception. They are trying to protect something that’s held within the music, even though the songs themselves collapse and snap back to it. 

There’s something candle-flicker-like about these songs. Their vulnerability is less a confession than a small, unstable light: a voice that falters, a recording that frays, a melody that bends to reveal sentiment without quite explaining what it is. That fragility embodies sincerity and introspection, without full transparency. A song can be sincere without the artist fully understanding what they’re expressing; it can turn inward without arriving at some essential truth about the self. It reminds me how I write — that I'll never land on a satisfying answer, but I will find a more attractive question.

We’ve become accustomed to treating vulnerability as evidence of authenticity, as though the disclosure of a private feeling grants us access to the person who feels it. In a culture where intimacy is so easily packaged and circulated, confession can become a performance. This music doesn’t always offer that resolution. Its feelings remain partially obscured, caught in distortion and fragments, intimate but not entirely available to us. It encouraging my instinct to float in the space between understanding and expression. Maybe it’s the ambiguity, not clarity, that feels vulnerable. Something just out of reach.

entry.title: Dominic Fike Shares New Single “Pangea,” Earns First Top 10 Hit With 8-Year-Old “Babydoll”
entry.summary: Dominic Fike is in crunch time of the rollout for a new album, but like so many musical artists today, he’s finding his greatest success from deep in his catalog. “Babydoll,” a track from his 2018 EP Don’t Forget About Me, Demos, caught a wave of popularity on TikTok this year and has since caught…
entry.content:
Dominic Fike is in crunch time of the rollout for a new album, but like so many musical artists today, he's finding his greatest success from deep in his catalog. "Babydoll," a track from his 2018 EP Don't Forget About Me, Demos, caught a wave of popularity on TikTok this year and has since caught on at radio. Today the song rises to a new peak of #10 on the Billboard Hot 100, becoming Fike's first top 10 hit.

Meanwhile, Fike's third full-length How To Quit Smoking is out next week, and he's promoting it today with the release of new single "Pangea." It's a breezy acoustic track that maintains Fike's signature genre-blurring ethos, merging the beachy sounds of Jack Johnson and Sublime with a more pronounced hip-hop influence. I feel like it would have been a hit in 2002, and judging by how things are going with "Babydoll," maybe it'll be a hit in 2026.

"Pangea" comes with a video featuring Fike in a seaplane over Vancouver during his recent tour, directed by his longtime collaborators Reed Bennett and Kevin Abstract. Watch below.

You might as well also check out prior single "Small Town." It matches Fike with Gabriel Jacoby and Emma Ogier, who caught our attention with her own recent single "Hands Tied." Like "Pangea," "Small Town" has a video by Bennett and Abstract.

How To Quit Smoking is out 10/30 on Columbia.
